final_answer.rationale: A "soft landing" requires two conditions: (1) inflation returning meaningfully toward 2%, and (2) avoiding a recession. On condition (2), the evidence is unambiguous — NBER has not declared a recession, real GDP grew every quarter from Q3 2022 onward, payrolls expanded continuously by ~8 million jobs, and unemployment rose only modestly from 3.5% to ~4.1–4.2%. On condition (1), core PCE inflation fell from its peak of ~5.8% in late 2022 to roughly 2.8–3.0% by late 2024 — a substantial decline of ~3 percentage points, clearly "meaningful" progress. However, the disinflation has stalled: the Dallas Fed in Sept 2025 noted headline PCE was still 2.7% YoY and core remained sticky, primarily due to housing services and non-housing core services. So the Fed achieved the recession-avoidance half cleanly, and most of the inflation half — but the "last mile" to 2% has not been completed. Whether this qualifies as a "full" soft landing depends on whether one requires hitting the 2% target precisely or just substantial progress. By most analyst and Fed communications standards (e.g., Powell's 2024 remarks), this is widely characterized as a soft landing in progress, though the AEI and others argue inflation may be getting "stuck" above target.

However, the lag relationship is NOT historically consistent: the 1970s episode fits the pattern, but the 2008–2014 post-GFC period is a major counterexample where similar (though smaller) M2 growth did not produce CPI acceleration. So M2 was a useful leading indicator in 2020–22 but is not a reliable one across regimes.
final_answer.evidence_summary:
FRED data, M2SL and CPIAUCSL (seasonally adjusted, monthly).

(1) 2020–2022 episode — M2 led CPI by 12–16 months:
- M2 YoY growth: Feb 2020 +6.8% → Apr 2020 +16.9% → Jun 2020 +22.8% → Dec 2020 +24.6% → Feb 2021 PEAK at +26.8% (15493→19642) → Dec 2021 +12.5% → Dec 2022 –1.0%.
- CPI YoY: Feb 2020 +2.3% → Apr 2020 +0.3% (COVID deflation shock) → Dec 2020 +1.3% → Mar 2021 +2.7% (acceleration begins) → Jun 2021 +5.3% → Dec 2021 +7.2% → Jun 2022 PEAK at +9.0% (270.654→294.957) → Dec 2022 +6.4%.
- Lag from M2 peak (Feb 2021) to CPI peak (Jun 2022): ~16 months. Lag from M2 acceleration start (~Apr 2020) to CPI acceleration start (~Mar 2021): ~11–12 months.

(2) 1970s episode — supports the pattern:
- M2 YoY ~+13% in 1971–72 (Dec 1971 710.3 vs Dec 1970 626.5 = +13.4%; Dec 1972 802.3 = +13.0%).
- CPI YoY surged from +3.4% (Dec 1972) to +8.7% (Dec 1973) and +12.3% (Dec 1974). Lag ~12–18 months.

(3) 2008–2014 — KEY COUNTEREXAMPLE:
- M2 YoY +9.6% (Dec 2008 vs Dec 2007: 8204.7/7483.9), continued elevated growth in 2009–2012 (Dec 2011 vs Dec 2010 = +9.8%).
- Yet CPI YoY stayed 1–2% through most of 2010–2015 (CPI Dec 2010 220.5, Dec 2014 236.3 = only ~1.7%/yr). No inflation surge despite multi-year elevated M2 growth.

(4) Research: Hanke & Greenwood (Johns Hopkins, May 2021 paper "Will the Pandemic Bulge in Money Cause High Inflation?") used the Feb 2020–Feb 2021 M2 growth of ~26.9% to forecast a CPI surge with a 12–24 month lag — a forecast that proved correct. St. Louis Fed ("The Rise and Fall of M2," May 2023) and Commonfund both note the 27% YoY M2 growth was the largest since 1959.

(5) Velocity matters: The post-2008 counterexample is typically explained by collapsing M2 velocity (banks holding excess reserves, weak credit demand). In 2020–22 velocity was supported by fiscal transfers directly to households, raising effective spending — which is why the M2 surge translated into CPI this time but not after 2008.
final_answer.rationale:
The user's question has two parts: (a) Did M2 lead CPI in 2020–22, and (b) was the lag "meaningful and historically consistent"?

Part (a) is unambiguous from the FRED data. M2 YoY growth accelerated sharply starting in April 2020 (driven by the Fed's balance-sheet expansion combined with massive CARES Act fiscal transfers that landed directly in deposit accounts) and peaked at ~26.9% YoY in February 2021. CPI inflation only began accelerating in March 2021 and peaked at ~9.0% YoY in June 2022. The 12–16 month lag is well-defined, "meaningful," and matches Friedman's classic "long and variable lags" framework. The Hanke/Greenwood 2021 paper made a real-time forecast using this exact relationship and was vindicated.

Part (b) — historical consistency — is where the case weakens. The 1970s clearly fits: elevated M2 growth in 1971–72 preceded the 1973–74 inflation surge by ~12–18 months. But the 2008–2014 period is a glaring counterexample where M2 grew nearly 10% YoY for multiple years yet CPI stayed at 1–2%. This is precisely why monetarism fell out of favor with most central banks after 2008 and why the Fed deprecated M2 as a policy target. The standard reconciliation is via velocity: in 2008–2014 QE largely sat as excess reserves at banks and M2 velocity collapsed, whereas in 2020 fiscal transfers put new money directly into household checking accounts that was rapidly spent.

So the honest answer: yes, M2 led CPI in 2020–22 with a clear, meaningful lag (~12–16 months) that was consistent with the 1970s — but the relationship is regime-dependent, not historically consistent across all episodes. It worked this time because the money creation was paired with channels that lifted velocity (fiscal transfers, no zero-lower-bound liquidity trap on household demand).

A monetarist-leading-indicator story and a supply-shock story are observationally similar with a 12–16 month lag.

Can the M2-to-CPI lag relationship be formalized in a model that endogenizes velocity, so that 2008–2014 (low velocity) and 2020–2022 (rebounding velocity) are both predicted rather than one being an exception?

Was the M2 signal actionable in real time, or only obvious in hindsight? Hanke/Greenwood made the call publicly in early 2021, but the Fed and most consensus forecasters did not — suggesting the indicator is contested even when it works.

How does the post-2022 M2 contraction (the first sustained YoY decline since the 1930s, reaching roughly –4% YoY in 2023) fit? CPI did decelerate, but not by as much or as fast as the symmetric monetarist prediction would imply.

Alternative anchors yield: Apr 2009 (quarter start) → adds ~2 months to all lags; mid-quarter (May 2009) → adds ~1 month. I report ranges to make this sensitivity transparent.

(1) UNRATE lag at trough: Using Jun 2009 reference, U-3 peak in Oct 2009 = 4 months (~1.3 quarters). Using Apr 2009 reference, lag = 6 months (~2 quarters). Importantly, U-3 stayed at 9.8–10.0% (within 0.2 ppt of the 10.0% peak) from Sep 2009 through Apr 2010 — a 7-month elevated band including a near-re-peak of 9.9% in Mar–Apr 2010. So while 10.0% in Oct 2009 is the unique maximum, the effective "peak region" runs ~Sep 2009–Apr 2010. Range: 1–3 quarters lag.

(2) PAYEMS lag at trough: The precise minimum is Feb 2010 (129,706), 8 months (~2.7 quarters) after Jun 2009. However, PAYEMS sat in a 351k plateau from Nov 2009 (130,057) through Feb 2010 — only 0.27% spread. If the plateau ONSET (Nov 2009) is used as effective trough, lag = 5 months (~1.7 quarters). If precise minimum (Feb 2010), lag = 8 months (~2.7 quarters). Using the Apr 2009 GDP reference instead, these become 7 and 10 months. Reasonable range: 2–3 quarters.

(3) U6RATE lag at trough: Dual peaks at 17.2% in Dec 2009 AND Apr 2010, with a dip to 16.6% in Jan 2010 in between. Lag = 6–10 months (~2–3 quarters) depending on which peak is selected. (4) Peak-side timing: PAYEMS Dec 2007 (138,395) and Jan 2008 (138,391) are within 4k of each other — essentially tied — and the series was clearly declining by Apr 2008. This near-coincidence with the NBER Dec 2007 peak is an empirical observation; PAYEMS is not formally designated "coincident" by NBER, but is one of six indicators NBER uses in dating cycles, which is why the alignment is unsurprising. Real GDP did not peak until 2008Q2 (16,943.29 > 16,915.19 in 2007Q4 by $28B), reflecting the 2008 stimulus-check PCE surge and export boom — an anomaly NBER explicitly looked past. Relative to the NBER peak, payrolls were essentially coincident (±1 month); relative to the GDP peak, payrolls "led" by ~2 quarters, but this is a framing artifact of the GDP anomaly, not an economic finding.

CONCLUSION: Using the standard NBER cycle reference, labor markets behaved as classic lagging indicators at the recession's end: U-3 lagged by ~1–3 quarters (Oct 2009 peak, with elevated plateau through Apr 2010); PAYEMS lagged by ~2–3 quarters (Nov 2009 plateau onset to Feb 2010 precise minimum); U-6 lagged by ~2–3 quarters with substantial dating ambiguity (dual 17.2% peaks Dec 2009/Apr 2010 plus oscillation through 2010). At the peak, payrolls were near-coincident with the NBER Dec 2007 reference; the apparent "lead" over GDP is a consequence of the well-known 2008Q2 GDP anomaly rather than a true business-cycle lead.

Quarterly GDP data cannot resolve the precise within-quarter timing of the 2009Q2 trough; using monthly NBER reference (Jun 2009) is the cleanest convention but introduces a small methodological choice.

Whether the 2008Q2 GDP local maximum should be considered a 'true' GDP peak or an anomaly is partly a definitional question; this analysis treats it as anomalous following NBER's own reasoning, but a purely mechanical GDP-based lead/lag analysis would yield different headline numbers.
